paper_title: SFT Conflicts, RL Coexists: A Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Multi-Task Learning for LLMs

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) exhibit fundamentally different behaviors in enhancing multi-task reasoning for large language models (LLMs). Our preliminary experiments revealed a phenomenon: SFT suffers from severe task conflicts under multi-stage training, whereas RL enables stable coexistence across diverse tasks. Empirically, we trace this to the parameter level, observing that RL induces sparse and approximately orthogonal updates across tasks. We provide a theoretical explanation for this mechanism by analyzing multi-task gradient interference. Our results reveal a distinction: interference in SFT is norm-limited, scaling with the absolute gradient magnitude, whereas interference in RL is variance-limited, bounded by the gradient variance induced by advantage normalization and on-policy optimization. This small variance bound yields near-orthogonal optimization directions across tasks. Leveraging this insight, we propose Parallel-RL, a paradigm that decouples multi-task training, significantly improving efficiency and flexibility.

Our preliminary experiments revealed phenomenon: SFT suffers from severe task conflicts under multistage training, whereas RL enables stable coexistence across diverse tasks. Empirically, we trace this to the parameter level, observing that RL induces sparse and approximately orthogonal updates across tasks. We provide theoretical explanation for this mechanism by analyzing multi-task gradient interference. Our results reveal distinction: interference in SFT is norm-limited, scaling with the absolute gradient magnitude, whereas interference in RL is variance-limited, bounded by the gradient variance induced by advantage normalization and on-policy optimization. This small variance bound yields near-orthogonal optimization directions across tasks. Leveraging this insight, we propose Parallel-RL, paradigm that decouples multi-task training, significantly improving efficiency and flexibility. Code 1. Introduction Enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) is central research focus, with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) as the dominant paradigms (Jaech et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). Recent works have explored their differences in single-task training (Chu et al., 2025; Matsutani et al., 2025). But their behaviors in multi-task settings, which is also crucial 1The Key Laboratory of Cognition and Decision Intelligence for Complex Systems, Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China 2School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China 3Tsinghua University, Beijing, China. Correspondence to: Jun Zhao <jzhao@nlpr.ia.ac.cn>. Preprint. August 7, 2026. Figure 1. SFT and RL exhibit significant differences during multistage training. SFT shows task conflicts, which impairs performance, while RL can steadily improve performance across tasks. for achieving Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), remain underexplored. We observe that in most existing works, researchers typically construct mixed datasets from multiple tasks for SFT (Dong et al., 2023; Park, 2025). In contrast, for RL, apart from using mixed-data training, many works commonly adopts multi-stage training, where each stage focuses on single task (Narvekar et al., 2020; Cho et al., 2024). To explain this divergence, we conduct comprehensive empirical and theoretical analysis comparing SFT and RL in multi-task training. We first tested the performance differences between SFT and RL when using mixed-data and multi-stage strategy for multi-task training. Table 1 reveals striking contrast: SFT suffers from performance collapses during multi-stage training, showing an average decline of 23.1% compared to the base model. Conversely, RL demonstrates robustness improvement (with gains of 24.9%) in multi-stage settings. Therefore, one of the key questions of our research is this significant difference: why SFT collapses under multi-stage training whereas RL achieves stable, cumulative performance growth on different tasks across multi-stage training? To answer this question, we examined the impact of single-task training on untrained tasks. As shown in Table 2, while SFT improves the target task, it causes substantial degradation in others. Conversely, RL enhances the target task while preserving performance on untrained tasks. We term this phenomenon SFT Conflicts and RL Coexists. This distinction in generalization directly answers SFT Conflicts, RL Coexists: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Multi-Task Learning for LLMs our inquiry. As illustrated in Figure 1, although SFT parameters updates are toward improving performance of each single task during single-stage training, severe conflicts arise across multi-stages, leading to performance collapse in the final multi-stage SFT model. In contrast, parameter updates induced by RL across different tasks are approximately orthogonal and can therefore coexist, enabling multi-stage RL to stably improve performance across tasks over stages. To understand the mechanisms behind these phenomena, we conduct an empirical analysis of the parameter updates , as detailed in Section 3. As illustrated in Figure 1, we highlight two observations. First, regarding the magnitude, RL induces significantly smaller updates, with an average magnitude over two orders of magnitude smaller than that of SFT. Second, regarding the interference between different , the similarity of across distinct tasks is negligible for RL ( 105) but substantial for SFT ( 101). We then provide theoretical analysis in Section 4 to explain these observations by examining their respective gradient descent directions. Specifically, the two key differences between their gradients lie in the Advantage Function and Policy Source. Thus in Sections 4.1 and 4.2, we qualitatively analyze how the advantage function and the on-policy nature of RL drive the observed sparsity of and small interference between different tasks. Furthermore, in Section 4.3, we derive the upper bound of gradient interference between tasks. Our proofs demonstrate that SFT interference is norm-limited and depends on the absolute gradient magnitude. Conversely, RL interference is variance-limited and is bounded by the variance of multiple rollouts (caused by both advantage function and on-policy). This theorem clarifies the distinct interference levels in multi-task settings and reflects the fundamental objectives of SFT and RL. Building on the insight that RL optimization directions across tasks exhibit approximate orthogonality, we propose Parallel-RL, novel paradigm for multi-task RL. In this framework, tasks are trained independently in parallel and their updates are subsequently merged. Experiments show that Parallel-RL matches single-task performance while improving training efficiency, and ablation studies further confirm its ability to effectively decouple task-specific capabilities. Guided by our analysis, we note that Parallel-RL goes beyond model merging and additionally requires techniques for task selection and single-task training. 2. Preliminaries In this section, we aim to provide preliminary evidence revealing the fundamental differences between SFT and RL in multi-task training paradigms, and to demonstrate their generalization on other tasks when trained on single task. 2.1. Experiment Setup We employ DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B as our base model. Our experiments cover four representative reasoning domains: math, science, coding, and logic. For RL, we adopt the GRPO algorithm (Guo et al., 2025). We utilized LoRA to facilitate efficient fine-tuning and analysis for both RL and SFT. Here we select MATH500, MMLU, Knights & Knaves, and LiveCodeBench as benchmarks for Math, Science, Logic, and Code tasks, respectively. Implementation details are provided in Appendix A. 2.2. Differences of Training Paradigms There are two paradigms for multi-task learning: MixedData, which aggregates datasets from diverse tasks for joint training, and Multi-Stage, where the model sequentially learns distinct tasks in separate phases. For SFT, MixedData training has become the consensus approach to mitigate forgetting (Dong et al., 2023; Park, 2025). In contrast, while also utilizing Mixed-Data, RL often follows MultiStage paradigm (Narvekar et al., 2020; Cho et al., 2024). To understand this difference, we conducted an experiment comparing two strategies, with results presented in Table 1. Table 1. Accuracy (%) of SFT and RL with different strategies. Conversely, RL exhibits robust improvements in both multistage and mixed-data settings, achieving average gains of 24.9% and 12.6%, respectively. The relatively smaller gain in mixed-data RL may stem from factors such as gradient imbalance across tasks (Wu et al., 2025b), which is not the key focus of our work. We focus on the more striking disparity: why multi-stage SFT leads to performance collapse while RL sustains stable and significant growth? Generalization of Single-Task Training To investigate the underlying reason for the question above, we analyze the impact of single-task training on the models performance across other tasks. As shown in Table 2, while SFT improves the target task by an average of 4.0%, it comes at the cost of degradation in untrained tasks, resulting in an average decline of 5.1% across other tasks. In contrast, RL achieves superior average gain of 6.8% on the target task while simultaneously exerting positive influence on others, yielding an average improvement of 2.3% on untrained tasks. These observations indicate that SFT and RL differ fundamentally in how they affect other capabilities during learning on single task. This phenomenon, which we term SFT Conflicts and RL Coexists, directly determines their suitability for different paradigms in multi-task settings. Table 2. Parameter-Level Empirical Analysis To investigate the mechanism underlying the contrasting generalization behaviors during single-task training observed in Section 2.3, we analyze the parameter update dynamics. For each task Ti, we compute the parameter update vector Wi and evaluate two key geometric properties: the magnitude (L2 norm) and the pairwise cosine similarity between tasks. As visualized in Figure 2, we identify two fundamental distinctions between SFT and RL updates. Observation 1: The magnitude of RL updates is minimal 3 and sparse. The heatmaps reveal stark difference between WRL and WSF in scale: the average L2 norm of is approximately 3102 for RL, whereas it reaches 7.4 for SFT, showing difference of over two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, RL updates exhibit high sparsity; only about 20% of parameters in RL have magnitudes exceeding 105, compared to 93% in SFT. These results align with recent findings (Mukherjee et al., 2025; Shenfeld et al., 2025) that RL tends to make minimal adjustments. The sparse and small parameter changes in the high-dimensional parameter space are significant factor that makes the training of RL for different tasks less disruptive. Observation 2: The optimization directions of RL across different tasks are approximately orthogonal. We observe that the pairwise cosine similarity of between different RL tasks is negligible, averaging around 105. In contrast, SFT exhibits high similarity across tasks (on the order of 101 to 1.0), with some updates even pointing in opposite directions (e.g., Math vs. Code). Consequently, the Wi for task Ti obtained from RL training can be considered practically orthogonal, resulting in minimal interference with the optimization landscapes of other tasks. Whereas the Wi from SFT exhibit overlapping optimization directions, which leads to significant mutual interference and the observed catastrophic forgetting. Overall, this empirical analysis shows that RL induces sparser and nearly orthogonal parameter updates across tasks, which are two key factors that explain its minimal interference with other tasks. Takeaway Unlike SFT, RL induces sparse, minimal updates that are approximately orthogonal across tasks, naturally decoupling the optimization of different tasks. This parametric mechanism fundamentally explains why RL supports robust multi-stage training. 4. Methodology Our preceding empirical and theoretical analyses establish fundamental geometric property of multi-task RL: parameter updates for distinct reasoning tasks occupy approximately orthogonal subspaces (Section 4). This finding implies that the interference term Wi, Wj is negligible. Considering optimization directions are irrelevant, the sum of parameter updates obtained from parallel training of different tasks should theoretically approximate the result of multi-stage training of tasks. Motivated by this insight, we propose Parallel-RL, decoupled post-training paradigm. In Parallel-RL, we can optimize each task independently. Formally, let = {T1, . . . , TN } be set of diverse reasoning tasks. We launch parallel RL training processes. Each process produces task-specific update Wi. The final model parameter Wf inal is obtained by merging these independent updates: Wf inal = Wbase + M(W1, . . . , WN ) where is merging function (e.g., linear averaging or SVD, discussed in Section 5.2). We emphasize that ParallelRL is not merely model merging technique, but complete post-training paradigm. Beyond the merging stage, it also involves determining which tasks can be trained in parallel, as well as adopting appropriate tricks for each single task training, which are preliminarily discussed in Appendix D. 5.2. Main Experiment Setup. We adopt DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 7B as the base models for full parameter training. The configuration follows the settings described in Appendix A. Here we choose GRPO as the RL algorithm. Results for other RL algorithms can be found in Appendix E.2. Parallel-RL Method. We explore several basic strategies for implementing and merging on Parallel-RL. (1) Naive 7 SFT Conflicts, RL Coexists: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Multi-Task Learning for LLMs Parallel-RL.We employ two strategies: (a) sum: directly summing the Wi, (b) mean: averaging the Wi. (2) Sparse Parallel. Two sparsification strategies are considered here. First, we adopt the standard TIES method (Yadav et al., 2023). Second, motivated by evidence that the rank-1 component of Wi encapsulates most RL training effects (Cai et al., 2025), we perform SVD on each update and retain only the rank-1 directions for merging. (3) Adapted Parallel-RL. Since different RL models enhance the sampling probability of high-reward trajectory for their respective tasks, the merged model can benefit from light post-merge adaptation. Main Results 6. Related Work As shown in Table 4, we observe that even Naive ParallelRL (sum) allows different task updates (Wi) to coexist, largely preserving the performance gains (95%) from single task training and achieving an average improvement of 5.0% over the base model. In contrast, Parallel-SFT (sum) suffers from severe task conflicts, with only 66% of the performance of the corresponding single-task SFT retained. Furthermore, incorporating sparsification strategies further enhances the compatibility of various Wi for RL. TIES and SVD Parallel-RL respectively retained 98% and 96% of the performance of the corresponding single-task RL. Notably, Adapted Parallel-RL achieves the best performance across most tasks. It delivers 9.4% gain over the base model and even surpasses individual task-specific models, retaining an average of 102.8% of the Single-Task RL performance. Despite these gains, this paradigm only needs an additional 5% samples adaptation time compared to single-task training, demonstrating both the efficiency and superior efficacy of our approach. More experimental results are available in Appendix E.1. We also performed Pass@K analysis to further verify the stability of Parallel RL, as shown in Appendix E.4. 5.4. Ablation Study To intuitively assess the orthogonality and decoupling of the learned task representations, we conduct an ablation study by selectively excluding each task-specific update (Wi) during the merging process. As reported in Table 5, removing specific Wi leads to significant performance drop in its corresponding task, with an average drop (T arget) of 7.1%. However, In contrast, the performance on the remaining tasks stays remarkably robust, even exhibiting slight average improvement (Others) of 0.6%. This result demonstrates that Parallel-RL effectively decouples capabilities across tasks. Unlike multi-stage or mixed-data RL, this paradigm allows for the flexible composition of models, enabling modular adaptation to diverse task scenarios. More We summarize research aligned with our core investigation and provide comprehensive discussion in Appendix B. Enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs has become focal point of recent research (Guo et al., 2025; Jaech et al., 2024). The dominant training strategies remain SFT (Xu et al., 2025; Hugging Face, 2025) and RL (Zheng et al., 2025; Ouyang et al., 2022). Recently, significant efforts have been made to distinguish the mechanisms of SFT and RL in single-task settings. Chu et al. (2025) argue that SFT memorizes, RL generalizes, suggesting SFT focuses on learning new paths, while RL enhances generalization. Similar works include (Matsutani et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025a), etc. There is also work (Mukherjee et al., 2025) pointing out that compared to SFT, RL training only finetunes the small subnetwork. Other works have explored the combination of these two paradigms (Zhang et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025). Multi-task learning is also essential for scaling towards AGI (Zeng et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025a). However, the divergence between multi-task SFT and RL remains underexplored. Some works have explored related aspects. RLs Razor (Shenfeld et al., 2025) theoretically explains that RL minimizes parameter deviation due to implicit KL constraints, thereby reducing forgetting. Similar analysis can be found in The Path Not Taken (Zhu et al., 2025). However, their analysis targets forgetting rather than multitask learning and the fundamental differences in the training paradigms. In contrast, our work is the first to systematically investigate the divergence between SFT and RL in multitask training with theoretical and empirical analysis. 7. Conclusion This work systematically analyzes the divergence between SFT and RL in multi-task training. We observe that in multi-stage training, SFT exhibits significant task conflicts, whereas RL demonstrates coexistence property, allowing for stable improvements. Through mechanistic analysis, we find that the optimization directions of RL across dif8 SFT Conflicts, RL Coexists: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Multi-Task Learning for LLMs ferent tasks share significantly lower similarity than SFT, appearing approximately orthogonal. We further substantiate these empirical findings with in-depth theoretical analysis, elucidating how the advantage function and onpolicy nature of RL drive this mechanism. Building on the findings, we introduce Parallel-RL to decouple multi-task training, enabling efficient, modular training that achieves superior performance with minimal adaptation.

sections.title: Impact Statements
sections.content: This paper aims to advance the development of multi-task learning for LLMs. By analyzing and improving the efficiency and effectiveness of model learning across diverse task scenarios, we hope to facilitate progress toward the vision of AGI. However, we emphasize that while striving for efficient multi-task training, it is also crucial to maintain the safety and reliability of each individual task to ensure responsible deployment. Finally, we believe that this methodological study does not introduce distinct ethical risks or societal impacts that warrant detailed discussion here.

Experiment Details A.1. Task and Dataset Description In this study, we select four representative tasks widely utilized in reasoning enhancement research for multi-task learning: Math, Science, Code, and Logic. In the following sections, we detail the training and evaluation datasets employed for each of these tasks. Training Datasets. We use different datasets that are more suitable for SFT and RL training, respectively. For SFT, we utilize subset of OpenR1-Math-220k (Hugging Face, 2025) as the math training set, subset of AM-DeepSeek-Distilled40M (Tian et al., 2025b) for code generation, and subset of AM-Thinking-v1-Distilled (Tian et al., 2025a) for science. For the logical reasoning task, we employ the knights-and-knaves (Xie et al., 2024) dataset. Since the original data lacks CoTs, we leverage the DeepSeek-R1 API to distill LongCoT data and ensure the correctness of the distilled answers using the rule-based verification logic from Logic-RL (Xie et al., 2025). Regarding RL, our training data consists of subset of the DeepScaleR-Preview-Dataset (Meng et al., 2023) for math and subset of the DeepCoder-Preview-Dataset (Luo et al., 2025) for code. For science, we use subset of the science portion from AM-Thinking-v1-Distilled. Finally, following the protocol of Logic-RL, subset of the knights-and-knaves dataset is used for the logical task. Evaluation Benchmarks. We evaluate our models using six mainstream and widely recognized benchmarks. For Mathematics, we select MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2023) and AIME2025. It is worth noting that the number of questions for AIME2025 is relatively small. To avoid randomness, we report the evaluation metric as avg@16, which is the average accuracy of 16 tests on the dataset. For Science, we employ MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021) and GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2023). Considering the massive scale of MMLU and the fact that some of its tasks are not directly related to scientific reasoning, we specifically focus on the following subjects: high school physics, high school chemistry, college chemistry, college biology, astronomy, and professional medicine. For Code Generation, we primarily use LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2024) for evaluation. Lastly, for Logical Reasoning, the knights-and-knaves dataset is used as the evaluation benchmark. A.2. Training Details We employ DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 7B as base models. All experiments are conducted on machine of eight NVIDIA A100 (80GB) GPUs. To facilitate efficient parameter analysis, some experiments are performed using LoRA (Hu et al., 2021). For all LoRA experiments, we set the rank to = 64 and the scaling factor to α = 32. For multi-stage training, we chose the following task order: Math, Science, Code, Logic. For TIES merging (Yadav et al., 2023), we follow the default settings and set the sensitivity parameter to 0.8. SFT. SFT is implemented using the LLaMA-Factory (Zheng et al., 2024) framework. We fine-tune the models on teacher CoT trajectories. The learning rate is set to 1 105, and the sequence cutoff length is configured at 8K tokens. RL. We utilize the VeRL (Sheng et al., 2024) framework for reinforcement learning training, specifically employing the GRPO algorithm. The RL learning rate is fixed at 3 106. Following the official DeepSeek configuration, we set the sampling temperature to 0.6 and top-p to 0.95. For each prompt, we generate = 16 rollouts to perform group-based relative reward estimation. The maximum output length is set to 8K tokens. Notably, we disable the KL divergence penalty in the loss function for our specific analysis. We acknowledge the exceptional contributions of LLaMA-Factory and VeRL teams. Their extensible and user-friendly frameworks, which support diverse architectures and advanced algorithms, significantly facilitated our training implementation. A.3. Evaluation Details For the majority of the tasks, we conduct evaluation using the lighteval (Habib et al., 2023) toolkit provided by Hugging Face. Consistent with the training configuration described above, we employ sampling temperature of 0.6 and top-p value of 0.95 for all model generations. For the logical reasoning tasks, we utilize the specialized evaluation suite from Logic-RL. We express our gratitude to the developers of these tools for their significant contributions to the open-source community, which ensured the reliability and comparability of our evaluation results. All evaluation experiments are performed on NVIDIA A100 (80GB) GPUs to maintain consistency in the computational environment. 13 SFT Conflicts, RL Coexists: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Multi-Task Learning for LLMs B. More Related Works In this section, we provide comprehensive review of the literature concerning post-training paradigms, the comparative analysis of SFT (Wei et al., 2021) and RL (Ziegler et al., 2019), and multi-task learning. Post-Training for Large Language Models. The mainstream post-training paradigms mainly include SFT and RL. In the era of reasoning enhancement, SFT has evolved beyond simple instruction following to incorporate Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methodologies (Wei et al., 2022; Jin et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b), which encourage models to generate step-by-step reasoning paths (Li et al., 2025b; Longpre et al., 2023). Recent advancements have further refined this approach through specialized reasoning fine-tuning, significantly boosting capabilities in mathematical and logical tasks (Xu et al., 2025; Hugging Face, 2025; Tan et al., 2026b;a). At the same time RL has shifted focus from traditional human preference alignment (Ouyang et al., 2022; Jin et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2026a; Men et al., 2025) to outcome-driven reasoning optimization. By leveraging verifiable rewards in domains like mathematics and coding (Hao et al., 2026), methods exemplified by DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025) and other recent frameworks (Yu et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2025a) have greatly improved the model reasoning capabilities (Li et al., 2026c; Men et al., 2026b). Comparative Analysis of SFT and RL in Single-Task Learning. representative comparative study (Chu et al., 2025) characterize the distinction as SFT memorizes, RL generalizes, observing that while SFT is responsible for fitting supervised training paths, RL focuses on generalization. Mechanistically, this divergence is often attributed to search space dynamics. Other work (Matsutani et al., 2025) propose that RL squeezes, SFT expands, indicating that RL contracts the policy towards high-reward regions, whereas SFT broadens the sampling space. Furthermore, Jin et al. (2025a) find that RL can recover generalization capabilities lost during aggressive SFT. Other research has also compared the differences between the two in terms of out-of-distribution (OOD) task generalization (Huan et al., 2025). There is also work(Mukherjee et al., 2025) pointing out that compared to SFT, RL training only fine-tunes the small subnetwork. Recognizing the distinct properties of RL and SFT, recent hybrid approaches integrate on-policy RL with off-policy SFT to leverage the benefits of both paradigms (Fu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Multi-Task Learning. To enable deployment in complex real-world scenarios, enhancing the multi-task reasoning capabilities of LLMs has become priority (Google, 2025; OpenAI, 2025; Yang et al., 2025). For SFT, the common practice is to train on mixed datasets spanning diverse tasks (Hugging Face, 2025). Existing studies suggest that conflicts in multi-task SFT are often severe and evolve throughout training, motivating adaptive data selection, curriculum design, and conflict-aware reweighting instead of static data mixing alone (Wu et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2025). In contrast, RL paradigms exhibit more diverse strategies. Many works explore multi-stage training (Zeng et al., 2025a), or employ curriculum learning strategies (Cho et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a) to progressively build capabilities. Other studies investigate mixed-data RL by alleviating gradient imbalance (Wu et al., 2025a) or scaling RL on heterogeneous reasoning data (Liu et al., 2025a). Recent multi-task RL studies further show that cross-domain transfer is highly dependent on tasks: while some domains are mutually beneficial, others induce negative transfer or capacity competition (Li et al., 2025c; Cheng et al., 2025). Complementary optimization-based methods further seek to mitigate such conflicts by improving gradient compatibility across domains (Liang et al., 2026). Despite these advances, the paradigmatic divergence between SFT and RL in multi-task settings remains under-analyzed. Recent studies demonstrate that RL exhibits significantly less catastrophic forgetting than SFT (Shenfeld et al., 2025; Lai et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025). In contrast, our work is the first to systematically investigate this divergence through both theoretical and empirical analysis. As the field evolves towards Agentic RL and the number of reasoning tasks continues to grow (Zeng et al., 2025b; Men et al., 2026a), understanding these fundamental differences is increasingly important for scalable AGI development. Model Merging Techniques. The paradigm of model merging has emerged as highly efficient strategy to integrate the capabilities of multiple expert models without the prohibitive costs of retraining. Foundational works in this domain demonstrated that models can be fused via simple weight averaging (Wortsman et al., 2022) or through Task Arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2022), which operates on task vectors to add or subtract specific model behaviors. However, directly combining multiple task vectors frequently leads to severe performance degradation due to task conflicts. To mitigate this, subsequent research introduced subspace and sparsification strategies. Most notably, TIES-Merging (Yadav et al., 2023) resolves interference by pruning task vectors based on parameter magnitudes and electing dominant sign direction to eliminate sign conflicts during aggregation. Following similar sparsification philosophy, DARE (Yu et al., 2024) randomly drops parameters and rescales the remaining weights to seamlessly assimilate homologous models. Beyond sparsification, other advanced methodologies calculate precise merging coefficients by evaluating parameter importance, utilizing tools such as the Fisher Information Matrix (Matena & Raffel, 2022) or closed-form statistical solutions for linear layers (Jin et al., 2022). 14 SFT Conflicts, RL Coexists: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Multi-Task Learning for LLMs C. In RL algorithms utilizing group-wise advantage normalization (e.g. GRPO), δS captures the intra-group policy divergence corresponding to single prompt. In contrast, within PPO, this term represents the deviation across the prompts of entire batch. Nevertheless, the core mechanism remains the same: the advantage term ˆA acts as high-pass filter that removes the high-magnitude common direction ( S). In GRPO, the filtered represents the common characteristics of the models responses to specific input. This common direction exhibits large magnitude because, given fixed model and input, the variance in model activations is inherently limited. Conversely, in PPO, the filtering applies to the common direction across all samples in batch. Intuitively, this common direction is weaker than that derived from single input. This results in PPO being more perturbative than GRPO during parallel training. Supporting evidence can be found in Appendix E.1. However, since samples within batch typically belong to the same task domain (e.g., mathematics or coding), this process still effectively filters out significant commonalities associated with task-specific features and linguistic priors. Consequently, the upper bound of interference in PPO is determined by the policy fluctuations within the specific task. Drawing from this analysis, we propose potential strategy to optimize PPO in future work: by generating group of rollouts for single input and constraining the scope of advantage normalization to these intra-group trajectories, PPO may potentially achieve orthogonality effects comparable to those of GRPO. Method for Judging Different Tasks As discussed in Section 5.4 of the main text, the efficacy of Parallel-RL is sensitive to the selection of parallel tasks. Not all task pairs qualify as coexist; certain tasks may exhibit great interference and are thus unsuitable for parallel training. In this section, building upon the analysis in Section 4, we conduct preliminary exploration into defining whether two tasks are independent and can be trained in parallel. Based on the qualitative analysis in Section 4.2, we found that in two different tasks, high-reward trajectories activate disparate neural circuits and patterns. Thus an intuitive method to verify this is to analyze the distributions of the score functions for the two tasks. Specifically, we visualize these distributions using t-SNE. Given that t-SNE is dimensionality reduction technique, the separation of score function distributions in the t-SNE latent space serves as practical heuristic for determining task coexistence. As illustrated in Figure 3 of the main text and Figure 6 in the Appendix E.3, the training data for the selected tasks in main experiment exhibit relative separation for RL, suggesting their suitability for parallel training. We selected SynLogic (Liu et al., 2025b), recent influential work that synthesizes data for logical reasoning games (e.g., Sudoku, Mazes), which we refer to as the Game task. We trained DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on this game task following the same protocol as the main experiments and subsequently merged it with the Math and Code models trained in Section 5.2, respectively. The results reveal significant interference between the Game task and both the Math and Code tasks. The results are shown in Figure 4 (c) and (d). Consistent with Table 4 in the main text, we primarily compare the performance of the merged Parallel-RL model against the corresponding task-specific model. Exploration Benefit: In single-task RL, increasing exploration and output diversity helps the model discover lowprobability but high-reward reasoning trajectory (Guo et al., 2025). Interference Cost: However, increased exploration also amplifies the diversity among the rollout trajectories generated for the same prompt, thereby enlarging the intra-group variance . According to Theorem 4.5, the interference between tasks rises accordingly. While high exploration benefits single-task training, it increases the gradient interference. This may cause greater conflicts and performance loss during the merging phase. Empirical Analysis. To verify this, we conducted an ablation study using sampling temperature τ to control exploration. Since τ directly affects the entropy of the policy πθ, it serves as an effective control variable. Based on preliminary tests, we set the temperature range to τ [0.4, 0.8]. We varied the rollout temperature for the Math Model training while keeping other tasks constant. We evaluated the accuracy of the Naive Parallel RL model on MATH500 and measured the negative log-variance ( log ) of the intra-group variance . Due to resource constraints, we performed this analysis using LoRA on data subset. As shown in Figure 5, the performance of Math Model improves as τ increases from 0.4 to 0.8. At the same time log consistently decreases. This indicates rise in intra-group variance and corresponding increase in the interference upper bound. Crucially, the Naive Parallel-RL performance exhibits non-monotonic trend: accuracy first increases and then degrades as τ grows. At low temperatures, interference is small but single-task learning is insufficient; at high temperatures, single-task performance improves but excessive inter-task interference degrades the merged model. This curve clearly illustrates the explorationinterference trade-off. Notably, around τ 0.65, Parallel-RL achieves the best performance, achieving an optimal balance between single-task capability and multi-task interference. This further shows that parameter updates Wi derived from RL on different tasks exhibit low coherence and high decoupling. E.4. Pass@K Analysis Accuracy evaluation can be sensitive to the decoding strategy. To provide more robust evaluation of the stability and reasoning capability boundaries of the Parallel-RL paradigm, we adopt the pass@k metric. This metric measures the probability that at least one out of generated samples for given problem is correct, serving as proxy for the models potential reasoning upper bound. In this section, we conduct pass@k analysis on the Naive Parallel-RL described in Section 5.2. Specifically, we select four representative benchmarks for our four tasks: AIME2025 (Math), GPQA Diamond (Science), Knights & Knaves (Logic), and LiveCodeBench (Code). For each task, we compare three models: the Base Model, the task-specific Single-Task RL model trained on corresponding task, and the Naive Parallel-RL model. To reduce variance associated with small sample sizes, we employ an unbiased estimation method (Chen et al., 2021; Yue et al., 2025). We do not strictly sample times. Instead, we generate larger pool of samples (n k) and compute the unbiased estimator: pass@k = 1 (cid:1) (cid:0)nc (cid:1) (cid:0)n where denotes the number of correct samples among the generations. In our experiments, we set the total number of samples to 64, which covers the largest value evaluated in our benchmarks. We primarily analyze the pass@k performance for the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 7B models trained via GRPO (full-parameter), as well as the 1.5B model trained via LoRA. The results are presented in Figure 7. 26 SFT Conflicts, RL Coexists: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Multi-Task Learning for LLMs Figure 7. This convergence indicates that their reasoning boundaries are nearly identical. This phenomenon provides strong evidence for the low interference between RL tasks and the inherent stability of the Parallel-RL paradigm; even simple parameter averaging does not disrupt the underlying reasoning mechanisms learned by individual RL modules. Furthermore, it is notable that for most tasks, the performance gap between Naive Parallel-RL and Single-Task RL becomes negligible at Pass@16. This observation indirectly validates the feasibility of Adapted Parallel-RL. Since our adaptation phase utilizes = 16 rollouts per prompt, the minimal gap at Pass@16 suggests that the models capability is preserved in the merged parameters. Consequently, small amount of adaptation data (e.g., 5%) is sufficient to realign the policy and fully restore performance, as confirmed in our main experiments (Section 5.2). F.
